summary: Defines a Telnet option giving a mechanism for extending the set of possible options. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet only has room for a limited number of optional features. This document saves one of the last numbers now so that many more features can be added later, and explains how two computers would agree to use them.

questions: how to add more telnet options
what is telnet extended options list
how many telnet options are there
subtitle: A Telnet option that reserves option number 255 so the option list can later be extended.

tldr.problem: Telnet option numbers fit in one byte, so eventually a 257th option will be needed and there is no number left to give it.
tldr.mechanism: The EXTENDED-OPTIONS-LIST option, EXOPL for short and numbered 255, reserves that number now and defines subcommands that negotiate a second list of options inside Telnet subnegotiation.
tldr.outcome: Negotiating options on the Extended Options List is not permitted unless both sides agree to EXOPL, since the default is not to allow it.

facts.label: Subcommand codes
facts.value: Same values as the Telnet commands, 250-254

today: RFC 861 is an Internet Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Reserving Option 255
sections.content:
Eventually a 257th Telnet option will be needed. The EXTENDED-OPTIONS-LIST option, abbreviated EXOPL, will extend the option list by another 256 options in a manner that is easy to implement.

The RFC proposes the option now, rather than later and probably much later, in order to reserve the option number 255.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet can hold only so many features. Taking one number now leaves room to add a whole second page of them in the future.

sections.title: Turning Extended Options On
sections.content:
EXOPL is negotiated with the usual Telnet commands. IAC DO EXOPL requests that the receiver begin negotiating options on the Extended Options List, or confirms that it is expected to. IAC WILL EXOPL requests permission to begin, or confirms that the sender will begin. IAC WON'T EXOPL refuses to negotiate or to continue negotiating, and IAC DON'T EXOPL demands that the receiver conduct no further negotiation of such options.

The default is WON'T EXOPL and DON'T EXOPL: negotiation of options on the Extended Options List is not permitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Both computers must agree before the extra features can be used. Without agreement, they simply do not use them.

sections.title: Subcommand Format
sections.content:
EXOPL has five subcommand codes: WILL, WON'T, DO, DON'T and SB. They have exactly the same meanings as the Telnet commands with the same names and are used in the same way. For consistency they carry the same values as the Telnet command codes, 250 to 254.

Once both parties have agreed to use EXOPL, negotiating a specific option looks like IAC SB EXOPL DO/DON'T/WILL/WON'T/<option code> IAC SE. If that option then needs further negotiation, the format is IAC SB EXOPL SB <option code> <parameters> SE IAC SE.
sections.plainLanguage: The extra features are asked for in a message carried inside another message, like a note tucked into an envelope.
